blocks.text: 1. Adjusted R²
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444059883-276519569.png

R², the previous topic, closed with a genuine, systematic weakness worth taking seriously: adding any additional feature to a model, evaluated on its own training data, can never actually decrease R², and it very often increases at least slightly, even when that added feature carries no real, genuine predictive information about the target whatsoever. Adjusted R² exists specifically to close this exact gap, by explicitly building a penalty for model complexity, the number of features actually used, directly into the metric's own formula.

With this adjustment in place, a genuinely useless feature can now correctly cause the reported score to decrease, exactly as it intuitively should, rather than staying flat or ticking upward the way plain R² allowed. This makes Adjusted R² the more reliable of the two metrics specifically whenever comparing models that use a different number of features from each other.
2. The Formula
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444059883-537014981.png

Adjusted R² starts from plain R², already covered in depth in the previous topic, and applies a specific correction based on two additional quantities: n, the number of observations, or rows, in the dataset, and p, the number of features, or predictors, the model actually uses. The formula is Adjusted R² equals 1 minus, the quantity 1 minus R², multiplied by n minus 1, divided by n minus p minus 1.

The key structural piece to notice is the denominator, n minus p minus 1: as p, the number of features, grows larger, this denominator shrinks, which makes the overall fraction being subtracted from 1 larger, which in turn pulls Adjusted R² downward. This is the precise mechanism through which the formula builds in a direct, mathematical penalty for model complexity, one that grows more severe as more features are added to the model.
3. How the Penalty Actually Works
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444059884-280670706.png

Every additional feature added to a model increases p by 1, which shrinks the denominator n minus p minus 1 slightly, which in turn makes the overall fraction subtracted from 1 slightly larger, pulling the reported Adjusted R² value downward, all else being equal. This downward pull represents the genuine cost, in terms of the reported score, of adding one more feature to the model.

For that downward pull to actually be overcome, and for Adjusted R² to increase overall despite adding a feature, the new feature has to improve the underlying plain R² by enough to outweigh this built-in complexity penalty. A feature that genuinely, substantially improves the model's fit to the data will clear this bar easily; a feature that adds little or no real predictive value will not, and Adjusted R² will correctly decrease as a direct, mathematical consequence, precisely the behavior plain R² could never exhibit on its own.
4. Revisiting the Useless Feature Demonstration

It is worth returning directly to the exact demonstration closing the previous R² topic: adding a genuinely useless, randomly generated feature to a model, one that carries no real relationship to the target whatsoever. There, plain R², evaluated on the training data, either stayed exactly the same or ticked upward slightly, purely as an artifact of the model gaining extra flexibility to fit training noise, never actually decreasing despite the feature's complete lack of genuine predictive value.

Adjusted R², applied to that exact same comparison, behaves correctly instead: since the useless feature does not meaningfully improve the underlying plain R² by enough to outweigh the added complexity penalty, Adjusted R² actually decreases when that feature is added. This is precisely the systematic bias plain R² could not detect or correct for on its own, and precisely the fix this topic's adjustment exists to provide, giving a concrete, worked demonstration of why the two metrics genuinely diverge in exactly this situation.
5. The Same Philosophy as Feature Selection

Adjusted R²'s entire underlying philosophy connects directly back to the Feature Selection module, covered much earlier in this course, whose central premise was precisely that not every available feature genuinely helps a model, and that some features actively hurt generalization by adding noise or unnecessary complexity without any real corresponding predictive benefit.

Adjusted R² gives that exact same philosophy a direct, quantitative expression as an evaluation metric: a model using fewer features but achieving a higher Adjusted R² is, by this metric's own explicit logic, the genuinely better, more parsimonious choice, even if that same model happens to have a slightly lower plain R² than a more feature-heavy alternative. This connects the evaluation side of regression modeling directly back to the feature engineering and selection principles already covered in depth earlier in this course.

blocks.content: A model with fewer, well-chosen features and a comparable or higher Adjusted R² is generally preferable to a more complex model with a marginally higher plain R², since the simpler model is more likely to generalize well and is easier to maintain, interpret, and deploy in practice.

blocks.text: 6. Comparing Models with Different Feature Counts

blocks.alt: Comparing Models with Different Feature Counts
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444059884-222093101.png

The single most important practical use of Adjusted R² is comparing two or more candidate models that use a different number of features from each other, a comparison where plain R² is structurally unreliable, since it will always favor whichever model has more features, regardless of whether those extra features genuinely contribute any real predictive value.

Adjusted R² handles this comparison correctly and reliably instead, since its built-in complexity penalty only rewards a model for having additional features if those features genuinely improve the fit by enough to outweigh the corresponding cost, making it the metric of choice whenever feature count differs meaningfully between the models being compared, exactly the situation plain R² cannot be trusted to judge fairly on its own.

blocks.text: 7. Adjusted R² Is Always Less Than or Equal to Plain R²

blocks.alt: Adjusted R² Is Always Less Than or Equal to Plain R²
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444059884-1220047.png

A useful mathematical fact worth knowing directly: Adjusted R² is always less than or equal to plain R², for any model with at least one feature. The two values are only ever exactly equal in the trivial edge case of a model using zero features at all, essentially the naive baseline itself, a case with little practical relevance beyond illustrating the boundary condition of the formula.

In every practical case involving at least one genuine feature, Adjusted R² will report a strictly smaller, more conservative number than plain R² does for that exact same model, reflecting the complexity penalty already built directly into its formula. This relationship is a useful sanity check: if Adjusted R² and plain R² are ever reported for the same model and Adjusted R² comes out higher, that is a clear, unambiguous sign of a calculation error somewhere in the pipeline.
8. A Direct Overfitting Signal
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444059884-917307594.png

Tracking both plain R² and Adjusted R² simultaneously as features are added to a model one at a time offers a genuinely useful, direct diagnostic signal for overfitting. If both metrics rise together as new features are added, that is honest evidence those new features are contributing real, generalizable predictive value to the model, exactly the kind of improvement worth keeping.

If plain R² keeps rising while Adjusted R² starts to fall or plateaus, that divergence is a direct, mathematical warning sign: the newly added features are improving the model's fit to this specific training data's noise and idiosyncrasies, without adding genuine, generalizable predictive signal, exactly the pattern that tends to precede poor performance on new, unseen data. This divergence-tracking technique is a genuinely practical, actionable way to catch overfitting as it happens, feature by feature, rather than only discovering it later during a separate validation step.
9. When Adjusted R² Is the Right Choice

blocks.alt: When Adjusted R² Is the Right Choice
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444059884-350180948.png

Adjusted R² is the necessary, correct choice whenever comparing models that use a different number of features, exactly the comparison plain R² handles unreliably, covered in depth earlier in this topic. It is also the right tool whenever deciding directly whether a specific new feature is genuinely worth keeping in a model, since its complexity-penalizing structure gives a direct, principled way to weigh added predictive fit against added model complexity.

It is additionally the more trustworthy metric to report whenever working in a feature-rich, high-dimensional setting, where plain R²'s systematic upward bias from simply having many features available could otherwise create a misleading illusion of strong model performance that a closer, more careful evaluation would not actually support.

blocks.text: 10. Worked Example
The example below computes both R² and Adjusted R² while incrementally adding features, including one genuinely useless random feature, directly illustrating how the two metrics diverge.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import r2_score

def adjusted_r2(r2, n, p):
    return 1 - (1 - r2) * (n - 1) / (n - p - 1)

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
n_samples = 100
X1 = rng.uniform(0, 10, size=(n_samples, 1))              # genuinely useful feature
X2 = (2 * X1 + rng.normal(0, 1, size=(n_samples, 1)))      # another genuinely useful, correlated feature
X_noise = rng.normal(0, 1, size=(n_samples, 1))            # a genuinely useless random feature
y = 3 * X1.ravel() + 1.5 * X2.ravel() + rng.normal(0, 2, size=n_samples)

feature_sets = {
    "1 useful feature": X1,
    "2 useful features": np.hstack([X1, X2]),
    "2 useful + 1 useless feature": np.hstack([X1, X2, X_noise]),
}

for name, X in feature_sets.items():
    model = LinearRegression()
    model.fit(X, y)
    r2 = r2_score(y, model.predict(X))
    adj_r2 = adjusted_r2(r2, n_samples, X.shape[1])
    print(f"{name}: R2={r2:.4f}, Adjusted R2={adj_r2:.4f}")

blocks.content: Watch how R² keeps climbing, or at least never drops, with each added feature including the useless one, while Adjusted R² can actually fall once the useless feature is added, exactly the divergence pattern this topic covers as a direct overfitting signal.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Adjusted R² corrects plain R²'s systematic bias by explicitly penalizing model complexity, the number of features used.
The formula shrinks a denominator as feature count grows, pulling the score down unless a feature genuinely improves fit enough to compensate.
A genuinely useless feature can correctly decrease Adjusted R², exactly where plain R² could never detect the problem.
It expresses the same not-every-feature-helps philosophy already covered in depth in the Feature Selection module.
It is the reliable metric for comparing models with a different number of features, where plain R² is structurally unfair.
Adjusted R² is always less than or equal to plain R² for any model using at least one feature, a useful sanity check.
Divergence between the two metrics, plain R² rising while Adjusted R² falls, is a direct, practical overfitting signal.
It fits comparing models of different complexity, evaluating individual features, and reporting in high-dimensional settings.
Next up: MAPE, which expresses error as a percentage, offering yet another lens: scale-independent, percentage-based accuracy.
